title: Good leg day vs Bad leg day
summary: NH contrasts the typical long, isolation-heavy, once-a-week leg day with a short minimalist session: open with a heavy knee flexion, follow with a hip hinge such as RDLs, then finish with isolation in giant sets. He argues for training legs at least twice a week, treats heavy soreness as a sign of low frequency, and uses the spare room on leg day for abs, calves, neck and other small muscles.
claims: Legs work as a group and cannot really be isolated; going beyond the idea of an isolation leg day gets more results, saves time and prevents injuries
Never open a leg session with leg extensions or hamstring curls; if you want a warm-up, do the main lift with less weight
Always open with a heavy lift, either a heavy knee flexion or a heavy hip hinge, with heavy relative to your strength and goals
In his gentleman split, heavy hip hinges and heavy knee flexions never go on the same day: the heavy hinge goes on back day and the heavy knee flexion on leg day
One to four heavy sets of the opening knee flexion already do about 70% of the session's work by hitting your baseline
Do one to three high-intensity sets to failure in a relevant intensity window, optionally two to three back-off sets of the same pattern, and that exercise is done
Leg press, then extensions, single-leg press, lunges, reverse lunges and more extensions is junk volume, often done to avoid the pain of intensity that could be over in 45 minutes
Heavy lower-body training done properly has never been dangerous
Training legs once a week is not enough; at least twice a week is the minimum to grow them, and low frequency keeps you in constant neurological adaptation, which is when injuries happen
Soreness does not correlate with growth; it signals undertraining and poor adaptation, makes leg day unpleasant and leads people to skip it
Upper-body days should have more exercises than lower-body days because the upper body has more small muscles, while lower days dominate in total tonnage
A heavy squat followed by Romanian deadlifts covers quads, glutes, hamstrings and lower back: three heavy squat sets and three or four RDL sets of 6-12
Four sets of RDLs beat four sets of hamstring curls or Nordic curls; isolation can complement the heavy lifts but never replace them
Do not superset the opening heavy knee flexion; the RDL can be supersetted with chin-ups, shrugs, calves or rear delt work depending on work capacity
Pro bodybuilders are largely to blame for the culture of endless leg isolation; it may work for them but not for naturals
A leg extension does not justify three minutes of rest; run isolation as a giant set, for example extensions, hamstring curls, calves, shrugs and an upper-back move
Splitting one high-volume leg day into three sessions across the week gives far more gains because every exercise can be recovered from
A minimalist leg day frees room for small muscles: calves, neck, traps, forearms, rear delts and abs belong on leg day
Train abs on leg day after the heavy bracing work, for example with leg raises and decline bench crunches
Athletes should place unilateral movements after the knee flexion and hip hinge, done fatigued with less weight and higher reps, instead of leg extensions
Program leg day together with back day; all lower-body lifts share a line of specificity, so the two days should feed each other through double progression
Being sore for seven days after leg day is a terrible sign unless you are a complete beginner; fix your frequency first

Example bad leg day: leg extensions 5x20, leg press 4x15, leg curls 5x20, Smith squats 4x15, glute bridges 4x20, calf raises 6x20, all with 3 minutes rest, which takes about 4 hours and gives a useless pump and week-long soreness

Example good leg day: squats 3x4-8 or 3x3; RDLs 3-4x6-12 or 3x6-10 with pull-ups AMRAP and leg raises; then glute ham raises 5x10-15, calf raises 5x8-15 and neck extensions 5x15-20, done in two hours with warm-ups
Template knee flexion slot: 3x3 or an evolving rep range (4x4-8, 3x6-10), or 4x6-12 or 5x5 for variations like pause, front or Zercher squats

Template hip hinge slot: 4x8-12 (manage load if good mornings follow squats) or a floor pull 3x6-10, never high-intensity deadlifts, paired with a vertical pull (AMRAP or 3x5 weighted) or a horizontal pull but no barbell rows

Template finishing giant set: a second knee flexion that spares the lower back (leg press, lunges, unilateral) 4-5x10-15, hamstring isolation 4-5x15-20, calf raises 5x8-15, plus any small muscle you want to bring up
